objectives: Build a consistent sign convention from the definitions of force, potential energy, electric potential, and membrane voltage, and explain how a concentration gradient and an electric field jointly determine net ionic flux.
Derive the Nernst equation from the electrochemical equilibrium of a single ion, handling the valence z, the inside-to-outside concentration ratio, temperature, and voltage sign correctly.
Map the lipid membrane, ion channels, and applied current onto a capacitor, conductance–battery branches, and a current source, then derive the membrane equation from charge conservation.
Distinguish the perfect integrate-and-fire model from the leaky integrate-and-fire model, and calculate their slopes, time constants, steady-state voltages, rheobase currents, and first-spike times.
State what the equivalent circuit, integrate-and-fire model, and action-potential mechanism each retain and omit, without interpreting model components as literal biological parts.
prerequisiteBridge: Electric charge may be positive or negative, and Coulomb force has both magnitude and direction. Potential energy U measures a system's capacity to do work at a position, with F=−∇U; the minus sign means that the force points toward decreasing potential energy. Electric potential φ=U/q is potential energy per unit charge, so the same potential difference produces opposite energy changes qΔφ for positive and negative ions. Throughout this lecture, membrane voltage is defined as V_m=φ_in−φ_out: if the intracellular potential is 60 mV below the extracellular potential, V_m=−60 mV. Begin every directional argument from this definition.

Diffusion arises from thermal motion in a nonuniform concentration: net particle flux runs from higher to lower concentration. If a membrane is permeable to only one ionic species, movement of a small number of ions separates charge across the membrane and creates an opposing electric field. At equilibrium, the chemical and electrical driving forces balance, so macroscopic net flux is zero even though individual ions continue to move in both directions. A logarithm converts a concentration ratio into an energy difference; an exponential converts that energy difference back into a concentration or probability ratio.

Only four circuit ideas are needed to begin: voltage is a difference in electric potential, current is the rate of charge flow I=dQ/dt, a capacitor obeys Q=CV, and a resistive branch can be written I=G(V−E), where G=1/R. Unit conversion is crucial: 1 pA/1 pF=1 V/s, and 1 V/s=1 mV/ms. The positive current direction must be declared. Here, inward depolarizing current I_e enters the right-hand side positively, whereas outward ionic current G(V−E), which removes charge from the membrane capacitor, is subtracted.

The first-order time-constant analysis from the previous lecture applies directly. For τ dV/dt=−V+V_inf, voltage approaches V_inf exponentially from its initial value. A threshold–reset rule adds discrete events to that continuous trajectory. Understand the continuous voltage evolution and discrete spike events separately before combining them. The model does not reproduce an action-potential waveform; it represents a spike by the threshold-crossing time, an abstraction suited to studying spike timing and firing rate.

diagnostic.prompt: If V_m=−60 mV and V_m=φ_in−φ_out, which side has the lower electric potential? On which side does a cation have lower electric potential energy?
diagnostic.answer: The intracellular electric potential is 60 mV below the extracellular potential. For a cation with q>0, U=qφ, so its electric potential energy is also lower inside.
diagnostic.explanation: First use the voltage definition to order the electric potentials, then multiply by the sign of the charge to order potential energies. The ordering reverses for anions, so “negative inside” alone cannot determine the direction of every ion.

diagnostic.prompt: Intracellular K⁺ concentration exceeds extracellular K⁺ concentration, and the Nernst equation uses ln([K]out/[K]in). Is the equilibrium potential positive or negative?
diagnostic.answer: Because z=+1 and the concentration ratio is less than 1, the logarithm is negative; therefore E_K is negative.
diagnostic.explanation: The K⁺ concentration gradient drives efflux. Preventing net efflux requires a negative intracellular potential that attracts K⁺ inward, so the inside-minus-outside equilibrium potential is negative.

diagnostic.prompt: A membrane capacitor has C=200 pF and receives a constant inward current of 100 pA. Ignoring all ion channels, what is dV/dt?
diagnostic.explanation: The 10⁻¹² factors in pA/pF cancel to give V/s, whose numerical value equals mV/ms. A constant current therefore produces a linear voltage ramp across an ideal capacitor.

diagnostic.prompt: In a leaky integrate-and-fire model, E_L=−65 mV, G_L=10 nS, and V_T=−50 mV. What minimum constant current places the subthreshold steady state exactly at threshold?
diagnostic.explanation: At threshold, dV/dt=0 requires the applied current to exactly balance the leak current. Because nS·mV=pA, any smaller current leaves the steady state below threshold.

modules.title: Electrochemical potential, membrane voltage, and Nernst equilibrium
modules.guidingQuestion: When an ion moves across a membrane down its concentration gradient, how does charge separation create an opposing electric field, and at what voltage does net flux vanish?
paragraphs: The cell membrane separates two conducting saline solutions. Most of the fluid on either side remains nearly electroneutral: membrane voltage requires only a tiny fraction of ions to separate at the membrane surfaces, not a cell interior filled with negative charge. The first page introduces the electrical sign convention through F=−∇U and φ=U/q, then defines V_m=φ_in−φ_out. A resting value near −60 mV means that the intracellular potential is lower. The same convention governs reversal potentials, channel currents, and action-potential diagrams.

A concentration gradient supplies the diffusive drive. Suppose only K⁺ channels are open and [K]in>[K]out. Random motion produces net K⁺ efflux and leaves the inside relatively negative. As charge separation grows, the negative intracellular potential attracts K⁺ back inward. The chemical drive remains outward while the electrical drive points inward. At equilibrium, their contributions to the electrochemical-potential difference cancel, yielding zero net flux—not an end to microscopic ion exchange.

For a dilute solution, the molar electrochemical potential of an ion is μ=μ⁰+RT ln c+zFφ. This is equivalent to the single-particle Boltzmann form in the source: q_c=ze, R=N_Ak_B, and F=N_Ae, so RT/(zF)=k_BT/q_c. At equilibrium, c_out/c_in=exp(q_cE/k_BT); taking the logarithm gives E_ion=V_in−V_out=(RT/zF)ln(c_out/c_in). For a cation, z>0 preserves the logarithm's sign. For Cl⁻, z=−1 reverses it.

An equilibrium potential is not the voltage that a membrane must have at every instant. It is the voltage at which the net current carried by one ionic species is zero. Away from E_ion, current direction depends on the driving force V_m−E_ion together with channel conductance. The source values—about +55 mV for Na⁺, −75 mV for K⁺, +125 mV for Ca²⁺, and −60 mV for Cl⁻—are illustrative physiological values, not universal constants. Nernst potentials vary with concentration, temperature, and activity, while the actual V_m depends on multiple permeabilities and dynamic gating.

This framework also explains the direction of an action-potential trajectory. Rapid Na⁺-channel opening pulls V_m toward the positive E_Na. Na⁺ inactivation and a delayed rise in K⁺ conductance then pull V_m back toward E_K, after which channel recovery and leak currents return the membrane to rest. Approaching a reversal potential does not instantaneously equalize ion concentrations: only a small fraction of the cellular ion reservoir crosses the membrane during one action potential.
keyPoints: Membrane voltage arises from a small separation of charge at the membrane surfaces; the bulk intracellular and extracellular solutions remain nearly electroneutral.
Nernst equilibrium is a zero-net-flux state in which chemical and electrical driving forces cancel.
The sign of E_ion is set jointly by the definition V_in−V_out, the concentration ratio, and the signed valence z.
A reversal potential is the zero-current voltage for one ionic branch, not the membrane voltage at every instant.

derivation.title: From the Boltzmann ratio on the source page to the Nernst equation
derivation.setup: Assume that the membrane is permeable to a single ionic species with charge q_c=ze, that temperature T is constant, and that the solutions on both sides are approximately ideal and dilute. At equilibrium, the electrochemical occupancies are compatible and net transmembrane flux is zero.

steps.title: Write the Boltzmann weight used on the source page
steps.explanation: The probability of a state decreases exponentially with its potential energy; the electric potential energy of one ion is its charge times the local electric potential.

steps.title: Relate the occupancy ratio to the concentration ratio
steps.explanation: The equilibrium occupancy of the same ion on the two sides is represented by their concentration ratio, with the transmembrane potential difference entering the exponent.

steps.title: Write the electrochemical potential on each side
steps.explanation: The two sides have μ_in=μ⁰+RT ln c_in+zFφ_in and μ_out=μ⁰+RT ln c_out+zFφ_out, respectively.

steps.title: Connect single-particle and molar notation
steps.explanation: Using q_c=ze, R=N_Ak_B, and F=N_Ae, divide molar energy by Avogadro's constant to obtain RT/(zF)=k_BT/q_c. Thus, the source's Boltzmann concentration ratio and the molar Nernst equation express the same physical equilibrium in two unit systems.

steps.title: Impose electrochemical equilibrium
steps.explanation: Zero net flux corresponds to μ_in=μ_out. The standard chemical potential μ⁰ is identical for the same ion on both sides, so rearrangement gives zF(φ_in−φ_out)=RT ln(c_out/c_in).

steps.title: Insert the membrane-voltage definition
steps.explanation: Use V_m=φ_in−φ_out and denote the equilibrium membrane voltage for this ion by E_ion.

steps.title: Solve for the equilibrium potential
steps.explanation: Dividing by zF yields E_ion=(RT/zF)ln(c_out/c_in). Because valence appears in the denominator, a divalent ion has half the voltage magnitude of a monovalent ion at the same concentration ratio.

steps.title: Connect the result to current direction
steps.explanation: Under a linear conductance approximation, I_ion=G_ion(V_m−E_ion). Current through this branch is zero at V_m=E_ion; away from that voltage, the sign gives the direction under the stated convention.

symbolNotes: N_A is Avogadro's constant, and e is the positive magnitude of the elementary charge. The signed valence z carries the sign of ionic charge, so q_c=ze.
k_B and q_c are per-particle quantities; R and F are per-mole quantities. Do not mix the two notation systems.
c_in and c_out are the intracellular and extracellular activities, or approximate concentrations, of the same ion. They must use the same units so that their ratio is dimensionless.
The valence z includes its sign: +1 for Na⁺ and K⁺, +2 for Ca²⁺, and −1 for Cl⁻.
E_ion uses inside potential minus outside potential. Reversing the voltage definition reverses the overall sign of the formula.
derivation.unitsCheck: RT has units J/mol and F has units C/mol, so RT/F=J/C=V. The concentration ratio and its logarithm are dimensionless; E_ion is measured in volts.
derivation.limitCheck: If c_out=c_in, the logarithm is zero and E_ion=0. Increasing c_out/c_in for a cation makes E_ion more positive. The ideal formula tends toward zero voltage as T→0, but a physiological model is not valid at absolute zero.

workedExample.title: Calculate the K⁺ equilibrium potential at body temperature
workedExample.problem: Use concentrations independent of the illustrative source values: T=310 K, so RT/F≈26.7 mV; for K⁺, [K]out=5 mM, [K]in=140 mM, and z=+1. Calculate E_K, then determine how it changes when extracellular K⁺ rises to 10 mM.
steps: The initial concentration ratio is 5/140≈0.035714, and ln(0.035714)≈−3.332.
After extracellular K⁺ rises, the ratio is 10/140≈0.071429 and its logarithm is ≈−2.639.
The new value is E_K≈26.7·(−2.639)=−70.46 mV, about 18.5 mV more positive than before—a depolarizing shift.
workedExample.result: Initially E_K≈−89 mV; doubling extracellular K⁺ shifts E_K to ≈−70.5 mV.
workedExample.sanityCheck: In both cases c_out<c_in and z>0, so E_K must be negative. Raising the external concentration moves the ratio toward 1 and reduces the magnitude of the potential.

selfCheck.prompt: If Cl⁻ had the same inside-to-outside concentration ratio, why would its equilibrium potential have the opposite sign from that of K⁺?
selfCheck.answer: In the Nernst equation, signed valence z appears in the denominator. For Cl⁻, z=−1 reverses the sign of the logarithmic term, reflecting the reversal of electric force for a negative charge.

pitfalls: Mixing [ion]in/[ion]out with [ion]out/[ion]in without changing the sign to match the voltage convention.
Using z=+1 for Cl⁻ and thereby obtaining an equilibrium potential with the wrong sign.
Interpreting zero net flux as no microscopic exchange, or interpreting a reversal potential as equal concentrations.

modules.title: The membrane equivalent circuit: capacitance, conductance, batteries, and KCL
modules.guidingQuestion: How does each biological membrane feature map onto a circuit element, and how does charge conservation combine those elements into a membrane-voltage equation?
paragraphs: The lipid bilayer separates conducting solutions and allows opposite charges to accumulate on its inner and outer surfaces, so it acts as a capacitor C. Ion channels provide selective conducting pathways; the number of open channels and their single-channel conductance combine into a conductance G. Each ion's concentration gradient sets a reversal potential E, represented by a battery in series with the conductance. An external electrode or synaptic input injects charge and is represented by a current source I_e. This equivalent circuit preserves relationships among charge flow and voltage; it does not claim that the membrane contains metal components.

For fixed C, Q=CV means that changing voltage requires changing surface charge. Differentiating gives dQ/dt=C dV/dt, and the definition I=dQ/dt therefore gives I_C=C dV/dt. Injecting 100 pA into a 200 pF capacitor produces a slope of 0.5 mV/ms. A capacitor alone does not set a steady state: as long as a nonzero constant net current persists, voltage continues to change linearly.

Under a linear conductance approximation, an ionic branch obeys I_x=G_x(V_m−E_x). Net current is zero at V_m=E_x, and the driving force grows with the distance from E_x. G_x may be constant, as for a passive leak G_L, or vary with voltage and time, as do G_Na(t,V) and G_K(t,V) in the Hodgkin–Huxley model. The battery E_x sets the zero-current voltage; conductance determines the current produced by a given driving force.

Apply Kirchhoff's current law at the membrane node: net current entering the capacitor equals applied current minus the outward ionic currents, giving C dV_m/dt=I_e−Σ_x G_x(V_m−E_x). Every term has units of current. A positive net sum deposits positive charge on the inner capacitor plate and raises V_m; a negative sum lowers V_m; a zero sum makes voltage momentarily stationary. This equation is the common backbone of the IF, LIF, and Hodgkin–Huxley models.

The Hodgkin–Huxley equivalent circuit on the third page contains the membrane capacitor, a leak branch, and variable Na and K branches. Conductance changes during an action potential make those branches compete: increasing G_Na pulls V more strongly toward E_Na, whereas increasing G_K pulls V toward E_K. “Pull toward” does not mean setting voltage instantaneously to a reversal potential; capacitance and every other open branch determine the rate and trajectory.
keyPoints: The lipid membrane maps to capacitance, ion channels to conductance, and concentration gradients to reversal-potential batteries.
I_C=C dV/dt follows from Q=CV and I=dQ/dt.
KCL combines applied current and all ionic branches into one voltage-dynamics equation.
Conductance sets the strength of attraction toward a reversal potential; capacitance sets how quickly voltage can change.

derivation.title: Derive the multichannel membrane equation from charge conservation
derivation.setup: The membrane has capacitance C, receives an applied current I_e defined as positive inward, and contains several ionic branches. Define branch current from inside to outside as I_x=G_x(V_m−E_x).

steps.title: Relate charge to voltage
steps.explanation: The relative charge on the inner membrane surface is Q=C V_m. Assuming that C is constant, dQ/dt=C dV_m/dt.

steps.title: Write conservation at the node
steps.explanation: The rate of increase of intracellular surface charge equals inward applied current I_e minus all branch currents flowing from inside to outside.

steps.title: Substitute the conductance branches
steps.explanation: Using I_x=G_x(V_m−E_x) gives C dV_m/dt=I_e−Σ_x G_x(V_m−E_x).

steps.title: Solve the constant-conductance steady state
steps.explanation: If every G_x is constant, set dV/dt=0 and rearrange to obtain V*= [I_e+Σ_x G_x E_x]/Σ_x G_x: a conductance-weighted reversal potential plus the offset caused by applied current.

steps.title: Identify the time scale
steps.explanation: With total conductance G_tot=ΣG_x, write the equation as τ_m dV/dt=−V+V*, where τ_m=C/G_tot. Opening more channels therefore shortens the time constant.

symbolNotes: By convention, positive I_e injects positive charge into the cell, while positive I_x carries positive charge from inside to outside.
G_x≥0 is branch conductance and E_x is that ion's reversal potential; G_x(V−E_x) may be positive or negative.
C is total membrane capacitance. If parameters are expressed per unit area, divide every term in the equation by membrane area.
derivation.unitsCheck: C·dV/dt has units F·V/s=C/s=A, and G·(V−E) has units S·V=A, so every term can be added in one KCL equation.
derivation.limitCheck: If all G_x=0, the equation reduces to the ideal capacitor C dV/dt=I_e and has no finite steady state. If one G_k greatly exceeds all other conductances while I_e remains finite, V* approaches E_k.

workedExample.title: Instantaneous slope and steady state of a two-branch membrane
workedExample.problem: Use E_K=−85 mV as the specified branch parameter for this independent circuit example; it need not equal the −89 mV obtained from a different concentration set above. Let C=200 pF, G_L=10 nS, E_L=−65 mV, G_K=20 nS, and I_e=300 pA. Find dV/dt at V=−60 mV and the steady state V*.
steps: The outward leak current is 10 nS·(−60+65)mV=50 pA.
The outward K current is 20 nS·(−60+85)mV=500 pA, so net inward current is 300−50−500=−250 pA.
Thus dV/dt=−250 pA/200 pF=−1.25 V/s=−1.25 mV/ms, so voltage is falling at this instant.
The steady-state numerator is 300 pA+10 nS·(−65 mV)+20 nS·(−85 mV)=300−650−1700=−2050 pA.
Total conductance is 30 nS, so V*=−2050/30 mV≈−68.33 mV and τ=C/G_tot=200 pF/30 nS≈6.67 ms.
workedExample.result: At −60 mV, dV/dt=−1.25 mV/ms; the steady state is approximately −68.3 mV and the time constant is approximately 6.67 ms.
workedExample.sanityCheck: The steady state should reflect competition among the two branches after the current-induced shift. Substituting V=−68.33 mV makes the total outward branch current approximately 300 pA.

selfCheck.prompt: Why does increasing one channel conductance change both the steady-state voltage and the speed of approach?
selfCheck.answer: It gives that channel's reversal potential more weight in the steady-state average and increases G_tot, which reduces the membrane time constant C/G_tot; voltage therefore approaches the new steady state faster.

pitfalls: Memorizing C dV/dt without declaring current directions, then mixing sign conventions across ionic branches.
Treating reversal potential E as if conductance created it. E comes from an electrochemical gradient; G sets current magnitude.
Forgetting that nS·mV=pA, or reporting pA/pF as mV/s instead of V/s or mV/ms.

modules.title: From perfect integrate-and-fire to leaky integrate-and-fire
modules.guidingQuestion: What firing behavior follows from threshold and reset alone, and why does adding a leak branch create a steady state, a rheobase current, and a nonlinear F–I curve?
paragraphs: The perfect integrate-and-fire model retains capacitance C and applied current I_e, with subthreshold equation C dV/dt=I_e. A constant positive current produces a linear ramp with slope I_e/C. When V reaches threshold V_T, the model records a spike and resets V to V_R. Spike times stand in for action potentials; the model does not reproduce waveforms generated by Na and K conductances. It converts input current into interspike intervals but has no resting attractor.

Moving from V_R to V_T requires ΔV=V_T−V_R. Under constant current, the ramp time is Δt=CΔV/I_e, so without a refractory period f=1/Δt=I_e/[C(V_T−V_R)]. Every I_e>0 eventually produces a spike, so the perfect model has no positive rheobase current and its F–I curve rises linearly from the origin. Real neurons, by contrast, may remain at rest under a weak constant input.

Adding a leak branch gives C dV/dt=I_e−G_L(V−E_L). Leak grows with the displacement of V from E_L and always pulls voltage toward E_L. With τ_m=C/G_L and V_inf=E_L+I_e/G_L, the equation becomes τ_m dV/dt=−V+V_inf. Under constant input, V(t)=V_inf+(V_0−V_inf)e^{−t/τ_m}; voltage approaches a finite steady state exponentially instead of rising without bound.

Spiking requires V_inf to lie above threshold. The boundary condition V_inf=V_T gives I_T=G_L(V_T−E_L). If I_e≤I_T, the steady state remains subthreshold and sustained current produces no periodic spikes. If I_e>I_T, the exponential solution gives the travel time from V_R to V_T. This threshold current emerges from the balance between input and leak; it is not an extra current rule inserted by hand.

LIF still omits the action-potential waveform, channel gating, adaptation, and absolute refractoriness, but it links biophysical circuit elements to spike events. Compare models term by term: perfect IF and LIF both contain capacitance, threshold, and reset; only LIF contains E_L, G_L, a finite steady state, and a positive rheobase. Identifying the responsible term lets you interpret an F–I change as a mechanistic consequence.
keyPoints: Perfect IF ramps linearly under constant current; every positive current eventually produces a spike.
The leak branch introduces τ_m=C/G_L and V_inf=E_L+I_e/G_L.
The LIF rheobase current is I_T=G_L(V_T−E_L).
Threshold and reset are event rules, not a simulation of the action-potential waveform.

derivation.title: LIF steady state, rheobase, and first-spike time
derivation.setup: Consider C dV/dt=I_e−G_L(V−E_L) with constant I_e, initial voltage V(0)=V_R, and threshold V_T>V_R.

steps.title: Define the time constant and steady state
steps.explanation: Rewrite the right-hand side as −G_L[V−(E_L+I_e/G_L)], then define τ_m=C/G_L and V_inf=E_L+I_e/G_L.

steps.title: Write the subthreshold solution
steps.explanation: This is a first-order linear system with steady state V_inf, so V(t)=V_inf+(V_R−V_inf)exp(−t/τ_m).

steps.title: Obtain the rheobase current
steps.explanation: A trajectory starting below threshold can cross only if V_inf>V_T. The boundary V_inf=V_T gives I_T=G_L(V_T−E_L).

steps.title: Solve for the threshold-crossing time
steps.explanation: Set V(t_sp)=V_T and rearrange to obtain exp(−t_sp/τ_m)=(V_inf−V_T)/(V_inf−V_R).

steps.title: Take the logarithm
steps.explanation: When V_inf>V_T>V_R, the ratio lies between 0 and 1, giving t_sp=τ_m ln[(V_inf−V_R)/(V_inf−V_T)]. Without a refractory period, the periodic firing rate is 1/t_sp.

symbolNotes: V_R is the reset voltage after each spike and V_T is the event threshold; neither is an ionic reversal potential.
V_inf is the constant-input steady state of the subthreshold equation when reset is disabled.
τ_m is capacitance divided by leak conductance. Increasing capacitance slows the response; increasing conductance speeds it up.
derivation.unitsCheck: C/G_L has units F/S=s; I_e/G_L has units A/S=V; the logarithm contains a dimensionless ratio of voltage differences; t_sp is a time.
derivation.limitCheck: As I_e approaches I_T from above, V_inf−V_T→0, t_sp→∞, and firing rate→0. For very large I_e, leak matters less during the short ramp and the result approaches the perfect-IF value C(V_T−V_R)/I_e.

workedExample.title: Compare subthreshold behavior and repetitive firing with the same parameters
workedExample.problem: Let C=200 pF, G_L=10 nS, E_L=V_R=−65 mV, and V_T=−50 mV. Apply constant currents of 100 pA and 200 pA. Determine whether each causes spiking; if so, calculate the first-spike time and the rate without a refractory period.
steps: The membrane time constant is τ_m=C/G_L=200 pF/10 nS=20 ms, and the rheobase is I_T=10 nS·15 mV=150 pA.
At 100 pA, V_inf=−65 mV+100 pA/10 nS=−55 mV, below −50 mV, so the trajectory never crosses threshold.
At 200 pA, V_inf=−65+20=−45 mV, above threshold. The threshold-time ratio is (V_inf−V_R)/(V_inf−V_T)=20/5=4.
Therefore t_sp=20 ms·ln4≈20·1.3863=27.73 ms. Each reset returns to the same voltage under the same input, so every cycle has the same duration.
Without a refractory period, f=1/0.02773 s≈36.1 Hz.
workedExample.result: At 100 pA, voltage approaches −55 mV without spiking. At 200 pA, the first interval is about 27.7 ms and the repetitive rate is about 36.1 Hz.
workedExample.sanityCheck: Because 200 pA is only slightly above the 150 pA rheobase, the rate should be finite and modest. Ignoring leak, perfect IF gives 15 mV/(1 mV/ms)=15 ms, correctly predicting a faster crossing.

selfCheck.prompt: Why does 100 pA eventually produce a spike in perfect IF but never produce one in the LIF model above?
selfCheck.answer: Perfect IF has no opposing leak, so positive current continues to charge the capacitor. In LIF, leak grows during depolarization until it exactly balances 100 pA at −55 mV, a steady state below the −50 mV threshold.
